newsitem.title: UK: Stray asteroids may cross Earth's orbit-scientists.
newsitem.headline: Stray asteroids may cross Earth's orbit-scientists.

text.p: More than 200 "stray" asteroids measuring over one km (0.6 miles) in diameter could be roaming the solar system and some of them could cross the Earth's orbit, scientists reported this week.

In a letter in the latest edition of Nature magazine, the scientists from Colorado and Arizona said the asteroids came from the so-called Trojan swarms, two important groups of asteroids orbiting the sun at the same distance as Jupiter.

The Trojan swarms were originally more numerous than the asteroid belt, wrote Carol and Eugene Shoemaker -- who spotted the stray comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 that collided with Jupiter two years ago -- and Harold Levison.
But the swarms have shrunk because the effect of gravity from giant planets like Saturn has shaken asteroids loose to roam freely through the solar system.

"We estimate there are over 200 escaped Trojan asteroids with diameters greater than one kilometre currently roaming the solar system, a few of which may be on earth-crossing orbits," said the scientists.
Their report was based on long-term analysis of the stability of the Trojan swarms.
The research showed Shoemaker-Levy 9 was unlikely to have been a Trojan asteroid because of its orbit.
Every year hundreds of meteorites fall to the ground, usually causing little or no damage.

But the force of an object measuring 90 metres (300 feet) across hitting the earth would have the same explosive power as a single nuclear bomb, and anything larger would increase the destructive effect dramatically.
A month ago an asteroid named Toutatis and measuring about three miles (4.8 km) across came within 3.3 million miles (5.300 million km) of Earth, or 14 times further away than the moon.
In astronomical terms, that was as good as a near miss.
An asteroid is believed to have hit the earth 65 million years ago in the Yucatan peninsula in Mexico, causing climatic changes which may have wiped out the dinosaurs.
Scientists have called for funding for a network of telescopes to warn of an impending asteroid strike.
